correctness.rationale: At almost every direction, differentiability of a support function gives a unique support point and tangential coordinate h'; the normal lines are parallel and their offset difference is |f'|. The support functions are Lipschitz, so zero distance is equivalent to constant f, hence to the indicated outer-parallel-body relation by support-function additivity. For the upper bound, the distribution f'' is a finite signed measure; the periodic finite-difference remainder integrated against its variation is bounded by a^2 TV(f'')/2, also for intervals exceeding one period. Optimizing the resulting 4 pi ||f||_infty/a + a TV(f'')/2 bound on the derivative integral gives the stated constant. Independently, periodic mollification and integration by parts give integral |f'|^2 <= ||f||_infty TV(f''), so the asserted constant is admissible but not optimal. The support-curvature measures have masses P(K), P(L), which gives TV(f'') <= P(K)+P(L)+2 pi delta. Equal perimeter implies mean f=0; the periodic variation is at least twice its oscillation, and for distinct bodies the oscillation strictly exceeds ||f||_infty. The normalized smooth narrow bump has half-variation 1 and sup norm tending to 1; choosing its amplitude sufficiently small preserves positive curvature and disk containment, and scaling gives sharpness at any fixed positive perimeter. The cosine perturbation has curvature radius at least 3/8, common perimeter 3 pi/2, delta=e_n of order n^-2, and distance 2 n e_n, excluding every larger small-distance exponent. The upper estimate is uniform at bounded distances, not a global pure square-root bound under arbitrarily large relative translations. The supplied quadrature and arithmetic checker was inspected, not executed; those tests are not the universal proof.

value.rationale: This quantifies what can be recovered in the ordinary Hausdorff metric from an established but degenerate normal-line distance, and where the converse loses regularity. The strict but sharp inverse ratio and the different high-frequency obstruction at the same perimeter give genuinely useful geometric limits, even for smooth bodies in a fixed disk. The value is not a new qualitative convergence argument or an optimal forward numerical constant.
